CausalChain: Chronic liver stress/oxidative damage -> increased m6A modification on specific lncRNAs -> alteration of lncRNA secondary structure -> shift in binding partners from tumor-suppressive factors to oncogenic regulators (e.g., increased EZH2/HuR interaction) -> epigenetic reprogramming of metabolic genes -> enhanced glycolysis/lipogenesis/glutaminolysis -> metabolic reprogramming promotes HCC cell proliferation and survival
Hypothesis: Modulating m6A modifications on lncRNAs alters their secondary structure and binding affinities, leading to epigenetic reprogramming of metabolic pathways that drive hepatocellular carcinoma progression. Targeting the m6A modification machinery may restore normal lncRNA function and metabolic balance, representing a novel therapeutic approach in HCC.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by metabolic reprogramming that supports its relentless growth and survival. Here, we propose that stress-induced N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modifications on specific long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) act as molecular switches that alter their secondary structure and binding capacity. These structural changes may redirect lncRNA interactions from tumor‐suppressive partners to oncogenic epigenetic regulators, such as EZH2 or RNA‐binding proteins like HuR. This altered binding, in turn, leads to the dysregulation of key metabolic genes involved in glycolysis, glutaminolysis, and lipogenesis, thereby promoting a metabolic environment conducive to HCC progression. By modulating m6A modification levels, it might be possible to restore the normal function of these lncRNAs and counteract the metabolic adaptations of HCC cells, offering a novel therapeutic strategy.
